standfirst: Three poor sisters, seventy billion won that is not theirs, and a family wealthy enough to own the outcome. For nine episodes it is the tightest thriller of its year. Then the last stretch goes slack: a good drama that ends like a makjang. And the relationship the show spends all season building never becomes one, which is the grievance you will still be carrying at the credits.

picks.why: The other great K-drama about a woman quietly assembling leverage against people who assume they are untouchable. Same pleasure of watching preparation pay off in public, the same interest in class as the real weapon, and a villain drawn with the same chilly domestic detail. Difference: it is one woman and one grudge held for eighteen years, so it is far more disciplined and far less plotty. No sisters, no missing money, no twist per episode.

For the money specifically. A conglomerate mapped from the inside, succession treated as bloodsport, and the satisfaction of a plan landing on a family that has never once been told no. Difference: the register is corporate satire rather than gothic, the lead is a man with a second chance rather than sisters with nothing, and the ending divides its own audience just as sharply as this one does.

If what gripped you was institutional rot: police, prosecutors and press all bought, and the slow work of proving something anyway. It is the show Little Women's plot mechanics are reaching for, executed without a single coincidence or resurrection. Difference: no family, no sisters, no melodrama at all. It is cold, procedural and completely airtight, which cuts both ways.

For the youngest-sister energy that Little Women never quite pays off. A woman goes inside the organisation that took her father and the show refuses to suggest she will come out whole. Eight episodes, no filler, and a fight choreography language that means every decision has a body cost. Difference: physical rather than financial, and no plan cleverer than walking straight at the problem.

For the twist appetite handled by better writers. Sixteen episodes of a small town where everyone is lying about something, structured so that every rewatch surfaces details you missed. If the plot holes here annoyed you, and they should have, this is the corrective. Difference: no revenge, no money, and no women at the centre. The satisfaction is understanding, not winning.

The unserious option, and it knows it. Victims the courts failed, an episodic revenge service, a satisfying beating roughly every second week. If what you actually wanted from the finale was for someone to simply be punished, this delivers that on schedule. Difference: pulp with no long game, no ambiguity and no cost to anybody you like.

against.title: SKY Castle
against.why: The default pairing because both anatomise wealthy Korean families and both have a magnetic manipulator at the centre. But SKY Castle is a satire about academic pressure, its violence is entirely social, and nothing is ever stolen. Little Women is a thriller about a specific pile of money. If you came for the chase, there is no chase.

against.title: Mine
against.why: The obvious pick for the rich-family-secrets overlap and the strong women. It is a slow domestic drama about wives inside a chaebol house, interested in marriage and identity rather than in leverage. The forward motion Little Women runs on is simply not its project.

against.title: Penthouse
against.why: Comes up because of a shared cast member and because both escalate hard. Penthouse is makjang by design and gleefully so. Little Women is a serious thriller that acquires makjang symptoms late. Expect one, get the other, and you will end up disappointed by both.
